content: The document titled A Step-by-Step Guide Introducing Rubella Vaccine into National Immunization Programmes provides a comprehensive framework for the introduction of rubella-containing vaccines (RCVs) into national immunization schedules. It is intended for use by national immunization program managers and their partners to support operational planning and implementation. 1. Acknowledgment of Support: The production of this guide was made possible through unspecified financial contributions, for which the Department of Immunization, Vaccines, and Biologicals expresses its gratitude. 2. Purpose of the Guide: To assist in policy discussions and operational planning for the introduction of rubella-containing vaccines (RCVs) into national immunization programs. To provide technical guidance, up-to-date references on global policies, technical justifications, strategic considerations, and laboratory guidelines related to rubella vaccine introduction. 3. Global Vaccine Action Plan (GVAP): Endorsed by 194 Member States of the World Health Assembly in May 2012, GVAP aims to eliminate measles and rubella in at least five WHO regions by 2020. The integrated vision of a world without measles, rubella, or congenital rubella syndrome (CRS) is supported by WHO, UNICEF, and other partners. 4. Rubella and CRS Elimination Goals: All six WHO regions have established measles elimination goals, and two regions have rubella elimination goals. The Americas region was certified as having eliminated endemic rubella and CRS in April 2015. 5. Rubella Virus and Transmission: Rubella virus is transmitted through person-to-person contact or respiratory droplets from infected individuals. The clinical diagnosis of rubella is unreliable due to its similarity to other febrile rash illnesses. 6. Clinical Presentation of Rubella: Rubella is typically a mild illness with a rash, often occurring in childhood or early adulthood. The incubation period averages 18 days (range: 12–23 days). Symptoms include low-grade fever, malaise, runny nose, and mild conjunctivitis, with lymph node swelling behind the ears and neck preceding the rash. The rash starts on the face and neck, spreading downward, and usually lasts 1–3 days. It is fainter than measles rash and may be difficult to detect on pigmented skin. 7. Complications of Rubella: Joint symptoms (e.g., arthritis, arthralgia) occur in up to 70% of adult women with rubella. Post-infectious encephalitis occurs in approximately 1 in 6,000 rubella cases. 8. Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS): Rubella infection during pregnancy, especially in the first trimester, can lead to miscarriage, stillbirth, or CRS. CRS is characterized by birth defects such as hearing impairment, blindness, congenital heart defects, and developmental delays. The risk of CRS is highest when infection occurs during the first 11 weeks of pregnancy, with up to 90% of liveborn infants affected. The risk decreases after 18 weeks of gestation. 9. Rubella Vaccine Introduction: Countries should leverage measles control and elimination activities to introduce RCVs. Strategies include switching to measles-rubella-containing vaccines (MRCVs), conducting wide-age-range supplementary immunization activities (SIAs), and strengthening immunization systems to achieve high coverage. Long-term commitment and financing are required to maintain at least 80% RCV coverage to reduce CRS incidence and eliminate rubella and CRS. 10. Vaccination Recommendations: The first dose of measles-containing vaccine (MCV) at 9 or 12 months of age should be an MRCV. A two-dose schedule of RCVs using the same combined MRCV is programmatically easier to implement. Immunization coverage of at least 95% is necessary for measles elimination and should be the target for rubella vaccination as well. 11. Pregnancy and Rubella Vaccination: Vaccination of pregnant women with RCVs should generally be avoided. No cases of CRS have been reported in over 1,000 susceptible women unknowingly vaccinated during early pregnancy. Rubella vaccination during unrecognized pregnancy is not an indication for abortion. 12. Surveillance and Monitoring: Rubella surveillance should be integrated with measles surveillance systems. Serological tests are required to ascertain immunity or susceptibility to rubella. Antenatal serological screening is a practical tool for monitoring susceptibility in pregnant women. 13. Key Considerations for Rubella Vaccine Introduction: Countries should assess the epidemiology of rubella, the burden of CRS, and prioritize rubella and CRS prevention as public health goals. Cost-benefit studies are not required in every country; data from similar settings can be informative. A preferred approach is to begin with an MRCV campaign targeting a wide age range, followed by routine MRCV introduction. This guide provides a structured approach to assist countries in evaluating their readiness to introduce RCVs and implementing the necessary strategies for success.
